assessment:
In this study, Medina-Feliciano and colleagues employ single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and hybridization chain reaction fluorescent in situ hybridization (HCR-FISH) to characterize the cellular composition of the regenerating intestinal anlage in the sea cucumber Holothuria glaberrima at 9 days post-evisceration. The authors set out to address a fundamental question in echinoderm regeneration: what are the cellular identities, origins, and fates of the progenitor cells that drive intestinal regeneration? This work represents the first application of these state-of-the-art techniques to adult echinoderm regeneration, providing unprecedented molecular resolution of a regenerative structure that has been studied primarily through histological approaches for decades.

The study identifies 13 distinct cell clusters from 3,844 cells, which segregate into three major categories: coelomic epithelial cells (7 clusters, ~70% of cells), mesenchymal cells (2 clusters, ~19%), and coelomocytes/immune cells (4 clusters, ~11%). The key findings include the identification of proliferating cells (C8), muscle precursors (C5), neuroepithelial cells (C9), and differentiating coelomic epithelial cells (C4), all localized to the coelomic epithelium. Most significantly, the authors identify clusters C1 and C3 as putative precursor cell populations that express pluripotency markers (PIWL1, YAP1, HES1) and appear capable of giving rise to multiple cell types. The characterization is strengthened by HCR-FISH validation of key marker genes (KI67, MYH7, STA10, HMCN1, FBCD1, BAR3, UNC5C, NET1, TRFM) showing appropriate spatial localization patterns. RNA velocity and pseudotime analyses support a developmental hierarchy where C1 represents the least differentiated state, giving rise to C3 and subsequently to differentiated cell types.

The evidence supporting the main conclusions is generally solid, with appropriate methodology including statistical validation of clusters, GO enrichment analysis, and spatial validation through HCR-FISH. However, the central claim of coelomic epithelial pluripotency, while well-supported by gene expression patterns and trajectory analysis, remains somewhat inferential without direct lineage tracing experiments. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation and present their conclusions as hypotheses supported by multiple lines of correlative evidence. The comparison to amphibian blastema is conceptually valuable, highlighting both similarities (expression of FGF, Wnt, TGF-beta signaling factors) and differences (spatial organization of proliferative and signaling cells). A notable limitation is that the dissociation protocol failed to capture mature muscle cells and neurons, potentially biasing the dataset toward more plastic cell types. Additionally, the lack of significant differences between anlage and mesentery clusters, while explained by the gradient nature of regenerative processes, suggests that finer temporal or spatial resolution might reveal additional cellular dynamics.

This work makes an important contribution to echinoderm regeneration biology by providing the first comprehensive molecular characterization of cell types in the regenerating intestinal anlage. The findings substantially advance our understanding of how the coelomic epithelium functions as a source of multiple cell types during organ regeneration, supporting the long-standing hypothesis of its pluripotent nature. The identification of specific precursor populations and their molecular signatures provides a foundation for future functional studies and comparative analyses across regenerative systems. While the study is primarily descriptive and some conclusions require additional experimental validation, the rigorous methodology, comprehensive characterization, and integration with prior knowledge make this a valuable resource for the regenerative biology community. The work will be of particular interest to researchers studying echinoderm regeneration, epithelial plasticity, and the evolution of regenerative mechanisms across metazoans.
